issues.legal_issue: The requirement to plead and prove readiness and willingness is met when the pleadings, read as a whole, convey that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform, even without prescribed words or phraseology.
material_facts: The plaintiff pleaded that he was always ready and willing to perform the agreement and described the steps he took to have the sale deed executed and registered.
The plaintiff had paid most of the agreed consideration, with the balance payable at execution of the sale deed.
The trial court and first appellate court found, on the evidence, that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.
issues.conclusion: The pleadings and evidence satisfied the readiness-and-willingness requirement; the High Court erred in finding otherwise based on the absence of specific words in the plaint.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires an averment and proof of performance or readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract. Under Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, pleadings must be read as a whole and compliance is assessed by their pith and substance; no particular phraseology is required unless the statute requires a particular form. Under C.S. Venkatesh v. A.S.C. Murthy, readiness and willingness may be inferred from the plaintiff’s conduct before and after suit and the surrounding circumstances; the plaintiff need not produce ready money but must prove means to generate the consideration.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The plaintiff brought a claim seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.pleadings_read_as_whole_convey_readiness: The plaintiff’s pleadings, considered as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform, even if they did not use prescribed words.
predicates.evidence_supports_ability_and_willingnes: The evidence, including the plaintiff’s conduct and capacity to meet the remaining obligation, supported readiness and willingness to perform.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance plaintiff’s pleadings as a whole convey readiness and willingness and the evidence supports the ability and willingness to perform, the readiness-and-willingness requirement is satisfied.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court should not disturb concurrent findings of fact based on the evidence unless those findings are perverse or contrary to the record.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court both found that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform, based on their assessment of the evidence.
The High Court reversed those concurrent findings in a second appeal because it considered the plaint’s averments insufficiently specific.
The Supreme Court found that the concurrent findings were neither perverse nor contrary to the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the proper scope of second-appellate review by reversing the concurrent factual findings on readiness and willingness.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 confines second appeals to the grounds permitted for such appeals. Concurrent findings of fact based on the evidence should not be interfered with unless they are perverse or contrary to the record.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision is under review in a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings_based_on_eviden: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual finding after considering the evidence.
predicates.findings_not_perverse_or_contrary_to_rec: The concurrent findings are not irrational or inconsistent with the evidence on the record.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, concurrent factual findings based on evidence that are not perverse or contrary to the record must not be disturbed.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance should not be refused through an unguided exercise of discretion where the agreement is proved, the plaintiff has performed substantially and is ready and willing to complete performance, and the circumstances favor the plaintiff.
material_facts: The courts below found that the agreement to sell was executed and proved, that a substantial part of the consideration had been paid, and that the plaintiff was ready and willing to pay the balance at execution.
The subsequent purchasers were found to have known of the agreement when they purchased the property, and the consideration stated in their sale deed was doubted.
The subsequent purchasers remained in possession and enjoyed the property during the prolonged litigation, while the plaintiff was kept out of possession.

The High Court relied on the discretionary character of specific performance to refuse relief, although no issue on that ground had been framed and no cogent reasons were given for refusing the decree.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s discretionary refusal of specific performance was unsustainable; the decree for specific performance was restored, and the subsequent purchasers’ possession and the passage of time caused by the litigation did not justify denying relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as applicable to the case, made specific performance discretionary, but that discretion had to be exercised judiciously, soundly and reasonably. Where execution is proved, part consideration is paid, and the plaintiff is ready and willing to perform, the balance should tilt toward the plaintiff rather than reward dishonest conduct by the defendant. The Court noted that the later amendment inserting Section 10(a), though not applied retrospectively, could guide the exercise of discretion; whether it applied retrospectively or to pending proceedings was left open. The Court also held that delay caused by prolonged litigation could not operate to the plaintiff’s disadvantage in the circumstances, particularly where the purchasers had notice of the agreement.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and agreement_execution_proved and substantial_part_of_consideration_paid and plaintiff_ready_and_willing and transferees_purchased_with_notice and equitable_circumstances_favor_plaintiff

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The plaintiff brought a claim seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.agreement_execution_proved: The evidence established that the agreement to sell was executed.
predicates.substantial_part_of_consideration_paid: The plaintiff paid a substantial portion of the agreed consideration before completion.
predicates.plaintiff_ready_and_willing: The plaintiff was ready and willing to perform the remaining obligations under the agreement.
predicates.transferees_purchased_with_notice: The later purchasers knew of the earlier agreement when they acquired the property.
predicates.equitable_circumstances_favor_plaintiff: The surrounding conduct and circumstances favored the plaintiff, including doubtful consideration for the later transfer or delay and deprivation caused by prolonged litigation.

issues.definition: When an agreement is proved, substantial consideration has been paid, the plaintiff is ready and willing to complete, and the later purchasers acquired with notice in circumstances favoring the plaintiff, specific performance should be granted.
